Incumbent one-term [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] Senator [[Marsha Blackburn]] defeated state representative [[Gloria Johnson (politician)|Gloria Johnson]] with 63.8% of the vote. Blackburn improved vastly from her [[2018 United States Senate election in Tennessee|2018 performance]] by nearly 19 points.{{Cite web |title=Dave Leip's Atlas of U.S. Presidential Elections - 2024 Senatorial General Election Election Results - Tennessee |url=https://uselectionatlas.org/RESULTS/state2.php?fips=47&year=2024&f=0&off=3&elect=0&class=1 |access-date=2026-04-08 |website=uselectionatlas.org}} The primaries took place on August 1, 2024, with Blackburn and Johnson winning their respective party nominations. This was the first general election for a Tennessee senate seat in which the two major party candidates were women.{{Cite web |title=Results for Women in the August 1st Primaries in Tennessee |url=https://cawp.rutgers.edu/blog/results-women-august-1st-primaries-tennessee |website=cawp.rutgers.edu}} Blackburn performed comparably to Donald Trump in the [[2024 Tennessee elections|general election]] overall but notably outperformed him in some key counties. Specifically, she outperformed him in [[Hamilton County, Tennessee|Hamilton]], [[Madison County, Tennessee|Madison]], and [[Shelby County, Tennessee|Shelby]]. She also outperformed Trump in [[Haywood County, Tennessee|Haywood County]]—a county he lost and where she had also previously lost—but this time, she managed to flip it. Johnson lost her home county, [[Knox County, Tennessee|Knox County]], by a wide margin.{{Cite report |url=https://sos-prod.tnsosgovfiles.com/s3fs-public/document/20241105GeneralbyCounty.pdf |title=State of Tennessee General Election Results, November 5, 2024, Results By County |date=December 2, 2024 |publisher=Secretary of State of Tennessee |access-date=December 2, 2024}} Although Johnson campaigned for the Senate seat, she simultaneously sought and won re-election unopposed to the [[Tennessee House of Representatives|State House]] in the [[2024 Tennessee House of Representatives election#District 90|90th district]].{{Cite AV media |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?si=Uck06VsK6srrov0y&v=fQGo1gwsSpo&feature=youtu.be |title=Rep. Gloria Johnson running for reelection in the TN House while also running for US Senate |date=2024-02-07 |last=WBIR Channel 10 |access-date=2024-08-27 |via=YouTube}} On August 6, 2025—just nine months after the election—Blackburn announced her candidacy for the [[2026 Tennessee gubernatorial election]].{{Cite web |date=2025-08-06 |title=Sen. Marsha Blackburn announces she's running for governor in Tennessee |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/politics-news/sen-marsha-blackburn-announces-running-governor-tennessee-rcna223338 |access-date=2026-04-08 |website=NBC News |language=en}}{{Cite web |date=2025-08-06 |title=Sen. Marsha Blackburn announces bid for Tennessee governor - CBS News |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/marsha-blackburn-tennessee-governor-campaign/ |access-date=2026-04-08 |website=www.cbsnews.com |language=en-US}} {{toclimit|3}} == Background == At the federal and state levels, Tennessee is considered to be a strongly [[Red states and blue states|red state]], having gone to Donald Trump by 23 points in the [[2020 United States presidential election in Tennessee|2020 presidential election]]. In Tennessee, [[Republican Party (United States)|Republicans]] occupied both [[Tennessee's congressional delegations#United States Senate|Senate seats]], 8 out of 9 U.S. [[Tennessee's congressional delegations#U.S. House of Representatives|House seats]], supermajorities in both state [[Tennessee General Assembly|legislative chambers]], and the [[Governor of Tennessee|governor's office]]. Due to Tennessee's strong conservative bent, this race was considered a "Safe" Republican hold. === Campaign === After defeating Former Governor [[Phil Bredesen]] by a surprisingly wide margin in [[2018 United States Senate election in Tennessee|2018]], Blackburn sought re-election. She was easily re-nominated as the Republican nominee. Initially, 2020 Democratic nominee for senate, [[Marquita Bradshaw]] was seen as the early favorite but months after her announcement, State Representative [[Gloria Johnson (politician)|Gloria Johnson]] entered the race. Johnson had gained prominence for her [[2023 Tennessee House of Representatives expulsions|protest]] on the Tennessee house floor over the [[2023 Nashville school shooting|2023 Covenant School shooting]]. Of the three representatives involved in the protest, two were expelled from the legislature, while Johnson narrowly avoided expulsion by just one vote. Johnson would go on to easily win the nomination. Throughout the campaign, Blackburn consistently led Johnson in the polls and enjoyed a significant financial edge, with a $9 million fundraising advantage. On October 16, the two candidates were scheduled to debate, but Blackburn declined to attend, leaving Johnson to face an empty chair.{{Cite web |last=Staff |first=MLK50 |date=2024-10-16 |title=U.S. Senate debate: Sen.
